introduction-the-distributed-needle-in-a.core: In microservices, one slow request may cross API Gateway, Lambda, three services, a queue and two databases. Distributed tracing follows the request end to end with a trace ID, recording timing for each hop, so you can find exactly where latency or errors originate. AWS X-Ray (and OpenTelemetry via ADOT) provide this.

first_principles.problem: p99 latency doubled, and each team insists its service is fine.
truths: Logs per service lack the full path.
A propagated ID links the pieces.

analogy.title: A parcel tracking number
analogy.story: Every depot scans the same number, so you see exactly where the parcel got stuck.
analogy.breaks: Parcels follow one path; requests fan out to many services in parallel.

example.title: Finding the slow hop
flow: Trace: API 20 ms → orders 30 ms → inventory 900 ms → DB 870 ms
Inventory's DB query is the culprit

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Root cause in minutes, no blame game.

check.q: What links spans from different services into one trace?
check.a: A propagated trace ID in request headers.

x-ray-architecture-the-daemon-the-udp-si.core: Instrumented apps send segment documents over UDP (port 2000) to a local X-Ray daemon or ADOT collector, which batches and forwards them to the X-Ray API. UDP keeps the app non-blocking. On ECS/EKS the daemon runs as a sidecar or DaemonSet; Lambda and API Gateway integrate natively.

first_principles.problem: Sending trace data synchronously from the app adds latency and failure modes.
truths: Managed services can emit traces themselves.

analogy.title: Dropping letters in a local postbox
analogy.story: You don't wait for delivery; the postal van collects and ships them in bulk.
analogy.breaks: Post is reliable; UDP can drop segments under extreme load.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: App traces flow with no request-path blocking.

check.q: Why does the X-Ray SDK send segments over UDP?
check.a: So tracing never blocks or slows the application's request path.

sampling-rules-managing-cost-noise.core: Tracing every request is costly and noisy. X-Ray sampling rules set a reservoir (fixed traces per second) plus a fixed rate (percentage beyond that), matched by service, method, URL path and host, with priorities. The default is 1 request/s plus 5%. Raise sampling for critical paths and errors; lower it for health checks.

first_principles.problem: Traces cost too much at 50,000 rps, and health checks dominate the samples.
derivation: Keep **reservoir** to guarantee some traces per second.
Use **tail-based sampling** (ADOT) to keep errors/slow traces.

analogy.title: Quality control sampling on a production line
analogy.story: Inspect a few items every minute, plus extra from the critical line.
analogy.breaks: Factory samples are random; head-based sampling decides before knowing if a request will fail.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No health-check noise; rich checkout traces.

check.a: The first request each second (reservoir 1) plus 5% of additional requests.

segments-vs-subsegments-the-anatomy-of-a.core: A trace is a tree. Each service that handles the request creates a segment (its work, with name, timing, HTTP data and errors), and within it subsegments record downstream calls (AWS SDK, HTTP, SQL) or custom code blocks. Subsegments for remote calls become inferred nodes in the service map.

first_principles.problem: A trace shows a service took 2 seconds but not which internal call caused it.

analogy.title: A project timeline with tasks and sub-tasks
analogy.story: Each department's task has sub-tasks showing exactly where time went.
analogy.breaks: Projects run sequentially often; subsegments can overlap in parallel.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: PDF rendering shows as its own 1.6 s block.

check.q: What creates inferred nodes in the X-Ray service map?
check.a: Subsegments for downstream calls to services that aren't instrumented themselves (e.g. DynamoDB, external APIs).

annotations-vs-metadata-making-traces-se.core: Annotations are indexed key-value pairs (string, number, boolean, up to 50 per trace) you can filter on with filter expressions (annotation.customer_tier = "gold"). Metadata is non-indexed, arbitrary data (objects, payloads) stored for viewing but not searching. Put business identifiers in annotations and debug detail in metadata.

first_principles.problem: Support asks for traces of a specific customer's failed orders, but nothing in traces identifies the customer.
derivation: Add **annotations** for searchable IDs (customer_id, order_id, tenant).
Add **metadata** for payloads and debug info.

analogy.title: Labels on folders versus notes inside them
analogy.story: Labels let you find folders fast; notes inside give detail once opened.
analogy.breaks: Folder labels are unlimited; X-Ray caps annotations per trace.

code.text:
xray_recorder.put_annotation('customer_id', 'c-42')
xray_recorder.put_annotation('order_status', 'failed')
xray_recorder.put_metadata('payload', order_dict)
# Console filter: annotation.customer_id = "c-42" AND fault

check.q: Which can you filter traces by: annotations or metadata?

the-x-ray-service-map-reading-your-archi.core: The service map is a live graph of services and dependencies built from traces. Each node shows request rate, latency distribution and error/fault/throttle percentages (colour rings), and edges show call relationships. It reveals hot spots, unexpected dependencies and cascading failures at a glance.

first_principles.problem: Nobody has an accurate diagram of how 40 services actually call each other.
derivation: Read **node colours** (red faults, orange errors, purple throttles).

analogy.title: A live traffic map
analogy.story: Red roads show congestion; you can see where a jam starts and how it spreads.
analogy.breaks: Traffic maps show physical flow; service maps only show sampled, instrumented calls.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Origin found by following red edges.

check.q: What does a purple ring on an X-Ray node indicate?
